  4. Equivalently (24 − 1)/2 = 15/2 = 7.5.

Answer: 7.5 slot times.

Common misconception. Answering 8 treats the range as 1 .. 16 or as 0 .. 16; the range is 0 .. 2i−1, which has an odd maximum and therefore a half-integer mean.

Takeaway. Expected backoff after collision i is (2i−1)/2 slot times — it doubles with every further collision.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which address in an arriving frame does a transparent bridge read in order to build its forwarding table?
questions.question_html:
Question 21MCQeasyethernet-standards-switches-bridgesstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which address in an arriving frame does a transparent bridge read in order to build its forwarding table?
options: The destination MAC address
The destination IP address
The frame's sequence number
The source MAC address
options_html: AThe destination MAC address
BThe destination IP address
CThe frame's sequence number
DThe source MAC address
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A transparent bridge learns by looking at where frames come from: if a frame with source address S arrived on port p, then S is reachable through p.

Step by step.

  1. The frame arrives on a port; the bridge records source → port in its table, refreshing the entry's age.
  2. It then looks up the destination address to decide where to forward the frame.
  3. So the source address is used for learning and the destination address for forwarding — two different reads for two different purposes.
  4. IP addresses are not examined at all by a layer-2 bridge.

Answer: Option (D) — the source MAC address.

Common misconception. Confusing the address used for learning with the address used for forwarding. Answering ‘destination’ describes the lookup, not the table construction.

Takeaway. Learn from the source, forward by the destination, and flood when the destination is unknown.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: What does a hub do with a frame it receives?
questions.question_html:
Question 22MCQeasyethernet-standards-switches-bridgesstandard textbookMarks: 1

What does a hub do with a frame it receives?
options: It forwards the frame only to the port on which the destination address was learned.
It discards the frame if the destination address is unknown.
It repeats the signal out of every other port, because it keeps no address table.
It rewrites the source address before repeating the frame.
options_html: AIt forwards the frame only to the port on which the destination address was learned.
BIt discards the frame if the destination address is unknown.
CIt repeats the signal out of every other port, because it keeps no address table.
DIt rewrites the source address before repeating the frame.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A hub is a physical-layer device: it regenerates and repeats electrical signals and has no notion of a frame, an address or a table.

Step by step.

  1. Bits arriving on one port are re-timed and sent out of all the others.
  2. There is no filtering, so every station in the collision domain sees every transmission.
  3. All ports of a hub therefore belong to a single collision domain and a single broadcast domain.
  4. Only a bridge or switch, which reads addresses, can forward selectively.

Answer: Option (C) — it repeats the signal out of every other port.

Common misconception. Option (A) describes a switch. Because a hub cannot read an address, it can neither filter nor learn, and it also cannot detect a collision per port — it merely repeats the collision to everyone.

Takeaway. Hub → repeat everything; switch → learn, filter and flood.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A switch receives a frame on port 1 whose destination MAC address is one that the switch has learned on port 1 itself. What does the switch do?
questions.question_html:
Question 23MCQmediumethernet-standards-switches-bridgesoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A switch receives a frame on port 1 whose destination MAC address is one that the switch has learned on port 1 itself. What does the switch do?
options: It filters the frame, that is, drops it, because the destination lies on the same segment as the source.
It floods the frame out of every other port.
It forwards the frame out of port 1 as well.
It returns the frame to the sender with an error indication.
options_html: AIt filters the frame, that is, drops it, because the destination lies on the same segment as the source.
BIt floods the frame out of every other port.
CIt forwards the frame out of port 1 as well.
DIt returns the frame to the sender with an error indication.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A switch compares the port learned for the destination with the port the frame arrived on. Equal means the two hosts share a segment and no other segment needs the frame.

Step by step.

  1. The source address is learned on port 1, refreshing that entry.
  2. The destination address is looked up and also resolves to port 1.
  3. Because the frame is already on the segment where the destination lives, forwarding it anywhere would be wasted bandwidth.
  4. The switch therefore filters — drops — the frame.

Answer: Option (A) — it filters the frame.

Common misconception. Believing a switch always forwards or always floods. Filtering is the third action, and it is what makes a switch a bandwidth-saving device rather than a repeater.

Takeaway. Three actions: filter if the destination is on the incoming port, forward if it is on another known port, flood if it is unknown.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about IEEE 802.3 Ethernet are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 24MSQmediumethernet-standards-switches-bridgesoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about IEEE 802.3 Ethernet are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A frame's payload must be at least 46 bytes for the frame to reach the 64-byte minimum.
Ethernet delivers frames reliably by acknowledging each one at the data link layer.
The preamble is seven bytes of alternating 1s and 0s followed by a one-byte start-frame delimiter.
A switch forwards a broadcast frame out of every port except the one on which it arrived.
options_html: AA frame's payload must be at least 46 bytes for the frame to reach the 64-byte minimum.
BEthernet delivers frames reliably by acknowledging each one at the data link layer.
CThe preamble is seven bytes of alternating 1s and 0s followed by a one-byte start-frame delimiter.
DA switch forwards a broadcast frame out of every port except the one on which it arrived.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. Ethernet is a best-effort, connectionless LAN: it detects errors but does not recover from them, and its frame format is fixed by the standard.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — the minimum frame is 64 bytes and the header plus trailer accounts for 18 bytes (6 + 6 + 2 + 4), so the payload floor is 46 bytes. Shorter payloads are padded.
  2. (B) False — there is no link-layer acknowledgement in 802.3. A lost frame is simply lost, and recovery is left to TCP or the application.
  3. (C) True — 7 bytes of preamble for clock recovery, then the 10101011 start-frame delimiter.
  4. (D) True — a broadcast address cannot be looked up, so the frame is flooded; the sending port is excluded.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. (B) is the usual error, often borrowed from Wi-Fi, where 802.11 does acknowledge every data frame. Wired Ethernet does not.

Takeaway. 64-byte minimum, 46-byte payload floor, 18 bytes of overhead, no acknowledgements.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question:
Four switches are cabled so that every pair is joined by exactly one link. The spanning-tree protocol runs and reduces the network to a tree.
How many of those links are left in the blocking state?
questions.question_html:
Question 25NAThardethernet-standards-switches-bridgesoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Four switches are cabled so that every pair is joined by exactly one link. The spanning-tree protocol runs and reduces the network to a tree.
How many of those links are left in the blocking state?

Answer format: an integer number of links.
questions.solution_html:
Concept. A spanning tree over n nodes has exactly n − 1 links. Every other link must be blocked, or a loop would remain.

Step by step.

  1. Four switches, every pair joined: the number of links is C(4,2) = 6.
  2. A tree on four nodes uses 4 − 1 = 3 links.
  3. Blocked links = 6 − 3 = 3.
  4. Each blocked port still receives bridge protocol data units but forwards no data, so the remaining three links form a loop-free path between every pair.

Answer: 3 links blocked.

Common misconception. Reporting 6 minus the number of switches, or blocking links until each switch has degree one. The tree requirement is n−1 links in total, not a star.

Takeaway. Blocked links = |E| − (|V| − 1) for a connected graph.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An IPv4 datagram has its IHL (Internet Header Length) field set to 5. What is the length of this header in bytes, and what is the largest header length the field can describe?
questions.question_html:
Question 1MCQeasyipv4-header-format-fragmentationstandard textbookMarks: 1

An IPv4 datagram has its IHL (Internet Header Length) field set to 5. What is the length of this header in bytes, and what is the largest header length the field can describe?
options: 20 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 60 bytes.
20 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 40 bytes.
5 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 15 bytes.
32 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 60 bytes.
options_html: A20 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 60 bytes.
B20 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 40 bytes.
C5 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 15 bytes.
D32 bytes; the largest header the field can describe is 60 bytes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. IHL is a 4-bit field that counts the header length in 32-bit (4-byte) words, not in bytes. The header must be a whole number of words because every header field is word-aligned.

Step by step.

  1. IHL = 5 means the header occupies 5 × 4 = 20 bytes.
  2. A 4-bit field can hold 0 to 15, so the largest expressible value is 15 words.
  3. 15 × 4 = 60 bytes, which leaves 40 bytes for the options field.
  4. The 20-byte figure is the minimum header, the one used when there are no options at all.

Answer: Option (A) — 20 bytes, maximum 60 bytes.

Common misconception. Reading IHL as a byte count gives 5 bytes, which is impossible; the field counts words. Reading the maximum from the options field alone gives 40 bytes, which is the size of the options, not of the whole header.

Takeaway. Any 4-bit length field in a header is in units of its natural word; multiply by 4 before comparing with an MTU.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A router receives an IPv4 datagram whose DF (Don't Fragment) bit is set. The MTU of the outgoing link is smaller than the datagram. What does the router do?
questions.question_html:
Question 2MCQeasyipv4-header-format-fragmentationoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A router receives an IPv4 datagram whose DF (Don't Fragment) bit is set. The MTU of the outgoing link is smaller than the datagram. What does the router do?
options: It fragments the datagram into MTU-sized pieces and sets MF on every fragment except the last.
It discards the datagram and returns ICMP Destination Unreachable with code 4 (fragmentation needed and DF set).
It forwards the datagram unchanged, because DF forbids the router from touching the datagram at all.
It holds the datagram in a queue until a link with a larger MTU becomes free.
options_html: AIt fragments the datagram into MTU-sized pieces and sets MF on every fragment except the last.
BIt discards the datagram and returns ICMP Destination Unreachable with code 4 (fragmentation needed and DF set).
CIt forwards the datagram unchanged, because DF forbids the router from touching the datagram at all.
DIt holds the datagram in a queue until a link with a larger MTU becomes free.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The DF bit is the sender's instruction that the datagram must reach the destination as one piece. It forbids fragmentation, not forwarding, so a router that cannot forward it intact must report the failure back to the source.

Step by step.

  1. The datagram cannot be fragmented, because DF is set.
  2. It cannot be forwarded either, because it does not fit the next link's MTU.
  3. The router therefore drops it and sends ICMP Destination Unreachable, code 4, carrying the MTU of the offending link.
  4. Path MTU discovery uses exactly these code-4 messages to lower the sender's segment size until the datagram fits.

Answer: Option (B) — discard and return ICMP Destination Unreachable, code 4.

Common misconception. Option (C) is the trap: DF does not mean 'forward without modification'. It means 'do not fragment', and a datagram that will not fit must be dropped and reported. Option (A) describes what happens when DF is clear.

Takeaway. DF set + datagram too big = drop plus ICMP code 4, never silent forwarding and never fragmentation.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An IPv4 datagram carries a 3000-byte payload. It must cross a link whose MTU is 1500 bytes; the standard 20-byte IPv4 header is used and there are no options. Every fragment except the last is filled with the largest multiple of 8 bytes that fits. How many fragments are produced?
questions.question_html:
Question 3NATeasyipv4-header-format-fragmentationstandard textbookMarks: 2

An IPv4 datagram carries a 3000-byte payload. It must cross a link whose MTU is 1500 bytes; the standard 20-byte IPv4 header is used and there are no options. Every fragment except the last is filled with the largest multiple of 8 bytes that fits. How many fragments are produced?

Answer format: an integer number of fragments.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The MTU limits the whole datagram, header included, so the payload a fragment can carry is MTU − 20 bytes, rounded down to a multiple of 8 because the fragment offset counts 8-byte units.

Step by step.

  1. Payload room per fragment = 1500 − 20 = 1480 bytes, which is already a multiple of 8 (1480 = 8 × 185).
  2. First fragment carries 1480 bytes; 3000 − 1480 = 1520 bytes remain.
  3. Second fragment carries another 1480 bytes; 1520 − 1480 = 40 bytes remain.
  4. Third fragment carries the remaining 40 bytes and has MF = 0.
  5. Total: 3 fragments, with payloads 1480, 1480 and 40.

Answer: 3 fragments.

Common misconception. Using 1500 as the payload per fragment forgets the 20-byte header and gives 2 fragments; using 1496 (the largest multiple of 8 below 1500) ignores the header as well.

Takeaway. Always subtract the IP header before rounding the fragment payload down to a multiple of 8.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An IPv4 datagram with a 4000-byte payload is fragmented for an MTU of 1500 bytes (20-byte header, no options). What is the value stored in the fragment offset field of the last fragment?
questions.question_html:
Question 4MCQmediumipv4-header-format-fragmentationoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

An IPv4 datagram with a 4000-byte payload is fragmented for an MTU of 1500 bytes (20-byte header, no options). What is the value stored in the fragment offset field of the last fragment?
options_html: A185
B1040
C370
D2960
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The fragment offset records where a fragment's payload begins, measured from the start of the original payload, in units of 8 bytes.

Step by step.

  1. Payload per full fragment = 1500 − 20 = 1480 bytes, a multiple of 8.
  2. Fragment 1: offset 0/8 = 0, carries bytes 0 to 1479.
  3. Fragment 2: offset 1480/8 = 185, carries bytes 1480 to 2959.
  4. Fragment 3: offset 2960/8 = 370, carries bytes 2960 to 3999 (1040 bytes, MF = 0).

Answer: Option (C) — 370.

Common misconception. Answering 2960 gives the byte offset but forgets the division by 8; answering 1040 gives the length of the last fragment, not its offset.

Takeaway. Offset field = byte offset ÷ 8. Keep the byte offset and the field value separate in your working.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The same 4000-byte payload is fragmented for an MTU of 1500 bytes, with a 20-byte header on every fragment. What are the values of the Total Length field of the three fragments, in order?
questions.question_html:
Question 5MCQmediumipv4-header-format-fragmentationoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

The same 4000-byte payload is fragmented for an MTU of 1500 bytes, with a 20-byte header on every fragment. What are the values of the Total Length field of the three fragments, in order?
options_html: A1500, 1480 and 1040
B1500, 1500 and 1040
C1480, 1480 and 1040
D1500, 1500 and 1060
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Total Length measures the fragment as it appears on the wire, header included. Only the last fragment is shorter than the MTU.

Step by step.

  1. Full fragments carry 1480 bytes of payload, so Total Length = 1480 + 20 = 1500 for each of the first two.
  2. The remaining payload is 4000 − 2960 = 1040 bytes.
  3. The last fragment therefore has Total Length = 1040 + 20 = 1060.
  4. So the three values are 1500, 1500 and 1060.

Answer: Option (D) — 1500, 1500 and 1060.

Common misconception. Option (C) reports the payload sizes as Total Length, dropping the 20-byte header. Option (B) forgets to add the header to the last fragment only, which is the most common slip.

Takeaway. Total Length always includes the header, on every fragment, including the last.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 6MSQmediumipv4-header-format-fragmentationstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The fragment offset field counts the position of a fragment's payload in units of 8 bytes.
The MF (More Fragments) flag is set in every fragment except the last one.
A fragment produced by one router may be fragmented again by a later router on the path.
Reassembly is performed by every router on the path, so the destination always receives a single unfragmented datagram.
options_html: AThe fragment offset field counts the position of a fragment's payload in units of 8 bytes.
BThe MF (More Fragments) flag is set in every fragment except the last one.
CA fragment produced by one router may be fragmented again by a later router on the path.
DReassembly is performed by every router on the path, so the destination always receives a single unfragmented datagram.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Fragmentation is a local repair made by whichever router meets a link that is too small; reassembly is end-to-end and happens only at the final destination.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. The 13-bit offset is in 8-byte units, which is why every fragment except the last must carry a payload that is a multiple of 8.
  2. (B) true. MF = 1 on all fragments but the last, and the last carries MF = 0 so the receiver knows the datagram is complete.
  3. (C) true. A fragment is just another datagram; if a later link has an even smaller MTU, that router fragments it again, splitting an already-offset range.
  4. (D) false. Routers never reassemble. All fragments carry the same Identification field and the destination reassembles them, which is why fragments may arrive out of order.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. The common error is to believe routers reassemble. Reassembly at every hop would need unbounded buffers and would destroy the independence of routes.

Takeaway. Fragmentation is per hop; reassembly is per destination. The Identification field is what ties the pieces together.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A 5000-byte IPv4 payload travels a path whose first link has MTU 1500 bytes and a later link has MTU 576 bytes. A router fragments only when it must, and every fragment except the last is filled with the largest multiple of 8 bytes that fits. The IPv4 header is 20 bytes on every link. How many fragments reach the destination?
questions.question_html:
Question 7NAThardipv4-header-format-fragmentationoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A 5000-byte IPv4 payload travels a path whose first link has MTU 1500 bytes and a later link has MTU 576 bytes. A router fragments only when it must, and every fragment except the last is filled with the largest multiple of 8 bytes that fits. The IPv4 header is 20 bytes on every link. How many fragments reach the destination?

Answer format: an integer number of fragments.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Fragmentation happens per hop, so the same payload can be cut twice. Each cut is governed by the MTU of the link in front of that router, and the second cut applies to each fragment produced by the first.

Step by step.

  1. First cut, MTU 1500. Payload room = 1500 − 20 = 1480 bytes, a multiple of 8.
  2. 5000 = 1480 + 1480 + 1480 + 560, so the first router emits 4 fragments with payloads 1480, 1480, 1480 and 560.
  3. Second cut, MTU 576. Payload room = 576 − 20 = 556 bytes; the largest multiple of 8 below 556 is 552.
  4. Each 1480-byte payload splits as 552 + 552 + 376, which is 3 fragments. Three such payloads give 3 × 3 = 9 fragments.
  5. The 560-byte payload splits as 552 + 8, which is 2 fragments.
  6. Total = 9 + 2 = 11 fragments.

Answer: 11 fragments.

Common misconception. The frequent error is to fragment the original 5000-byte payload once for the smaller MTU and answer 10 (since 5000/552 rounds to 10). That skips the first cut: the 576-MTU router never sees the original 5000 bytes, it sees four separate fragments.

Takeaway. On a multi-hop path, fragment counts multiply per hop. Work hop by hop, carrying the fragment list forward.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The address 172.16.5.9 is interpreted classfully, with no subnetting of the classful network. Which network mask applies?
questions.question_html:
Question 8MCQeasyclassful-vs-classless-cidrstandard textbookMarks: 1

The address 172.16.5.9 is interpreted classfully, with no subnetting of the classful network. Which network mask applies?
options_html: A255.255.0.0
B255.0.0.0
C255.255.255.0
D255.255.240.0
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Classful addressing fixes the split between network and host bits by the value of the first octet, and the class decides the default mask.

Step by step.

  1. First octet 172 lies in 128–191, so the address belongs to class B.
  2. Class B reserves 16 bits for the network and 16 bits for the host.
  3. The default classful mask is therefore /16, that is 255.255.0.0.
  4. Without subnetting, 172.16.0.0 is the network and 172.16.5.9 is one of its hosts.

Answer: Option (A) — 255.255.0.0.

Common misconception. Class D and E begin at 224, so 172 is safely inside class B. Confusing 172 with the private-range convention (172.16.0.0/12) is a different matter: /12 is a CIDR aggregate, not the classful mask.

Takeaway. Class A starts at 0, B at 128, C at 192, D at 224. Default masks: /8, /16, /24.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A subnet is described by the prefix /27. How many usable host addresses does it contain?
questions.question_html:
Question 9MCQeasyclassful-vs-classless-cidrstandard textbookMarks: 1

A subnet is described by the prefix /27. How many usable host addresses does it contain?
options_html: A32
B30
C14
D62
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A prefix of length p leaves 32 − p host bits, giving 2^(32−p) addresses. Two of them, the all-zeros network address and the all-ones broadcast address, cannot be assigned to hosts.

Step by step.

  1. Host bits = 32 − 27 = 5.
  2. Total addresses = 2⁵ = 32.
  3. Usable hosts = 32 − 2 = 30.

Answer: Option (B) — 30 usable hosts.

Common misconception. Answering 32 counts the network and broadcast addresses as usable. Answering 14 belongs to a /28 (16 − 2) and 62 to a /26.

Takeaway. Usable hosts = 2^(32−p) − 2 for any prefix shorter than /31; a /31 is the point-to-point special case with 2 usable addresses.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An interface is configured with the address 192.168.10.130/26. What is the network address of its subnet?
questions.question_html:
Question 10MCQmediumclassful-vs-classless-cidroriginal synthesisMarks: 1

An interface is configured with the address 192.168.10.130/26. What is the network address of its subnet?
options_html: A192.168.10.0
B192.168.10.64
C192.168.10.128
D192.168.10.192
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A /26 leaves 6 host bits, so consecutive subnets start every 2⁶ = 64 addresses in the last octet. The network address is the largest multiple of the block size that does not exceed the host octet.

Step by step.

  1. Block size = 2^(32−26) = 2⁶ = 64.
  2. Multiples of 64 in the last octet: 0, 64, 128, 192.
  3. The host octet is 130, and 128 ≤ 130 < 192, so the block is 128 to 191.
  4. Network address = 192.168.10.128; broadcast = 192.168.10.191; usable range 192.168.10.129 to 192.168.10.190.

Answer: Option (C) — 192.168.10.128.

Common misconception. Choosing 192.168.10.192 rounds up instead of down. Choosing .64 comes from assuming a /25 block of 128.

Takeaway. Block size = 2^(32−prefix); round the host portion down to a multiple of the block size to get the network address.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An interface is configured as 10.20.30.1/23. Which of the following addresses are usable host addresses on that same subnet? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 11MSQmediumclassful-vs-classless-cidroriginal synthesisMarks: 2

An interface is configured as 10.20.30.1/23. Which of the following addresses are usable host addresses on that same subnet? (Select all that apply.)
options_html: A10.20.31.255
B10.20.30.255
C10.20.29.10
D10.20.31.0
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A /23 borrows one bit from the third octet, so the subnet spans two whole /24 blocks. Only the very last address of the second block is the broadcast, and only the very first address of the first block is the network.

Step by step.

  1. Host bits = 32 − 23 = 9, so the block size is 2⁹ = 512 addresses.
  2. 512 ÷ 256 = 2 whole /24 blocks, so the subnet runs from 10.20.30.0 to 10.20.31.255.
  3. Network address = 10.20.30.0; directed broadcast = 10.20.31.255; usable range = 10.20.30.1 to 10.20.31.254.
  4. (A) 10.20.31.255 is the broadcast address, so it is not a host. False.
  5. (B) 10.20.30.255 is the last address of the first /24 block and lies strictly inside the /23, so it is an ordinary host. True.
  6. (C) 10.20.29.10 lies in the previous subnet, 10.20.28.0/23. False.
  7. (D) 10.20.31.0 is the first address of the second /24 block, also strictly inside the /23. True.

Answer: Options (B) and (D).

Common misconception. The trap is that .255 and .0 look like the boundary addresses of a /24. Under a /23 the boundaries move to .30.0 and .31.255, and every address between them, including .30.255 and .31.0, is a host.

Takeaway. For any prefix shorter than /24, work out the block boundaries in the subnet's own size; octet-boundary addresses are ordinary hosts.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An ISP is allotted the block 200.10.0.0/18. How many /24 networks does this block contain?
questions.question_html:
Question 12NATmediumclassful-vs-classless-cidrstandard textbookMarks: 2

An ISP is allotted the block 200.10.0.0/18. How many /24 networks does this block contain?

Answer format: an integer number of /24 networks.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Splitting a block into equal smaller blocks is a matter of comparing prefix lengths: each extra bit doubles the count.

Step by step.

  1. The allotted block has 18 network bits; each /24 has 24 network bits.
  2. The number of extra bits is 24 − 18 = 6.
  3. Each extra bit doubles the number of pieces, so the count is 2⁶ = 64.
  4. Check: a /18 spans 2^(32−18) = 16384 addresses, and 16384 ÷ 256 = 64.

Answer: 64 /24 networks.

Common misconception. Dividing 24 by 18, or taking 2^(24−18) but reading the result as addresses rather than networks, both lead astray. Another slip is to use 2^6 = 64 addresses instead of 64 networks.

Takeaway. Count of smaller blocks = 2^(longer prefix − shorter prefix).

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A router forwards using longest-prefix match against the table below. A packet addressed to 10.1.34.19 arrives. 10.1.0.0/16 → R1  ·  10.1.32.0/20 → R2  ·  10.1.34.0/24 → R3  ·  0.0.0.0/0 → R4 Which next hop is chosen?
questions.question_html:
Question 13MCQhardclassful-vs-classless-cidroriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A router forwards using longest-prefix match against the table below. A packet addressed to 10.1.34.19 arrives.
10.1.0.0/16 → R1  ·  10.1.32.0/20 → R2  ·  10.1.34.0/24 → R3  ·  0.0.0.0/0 → R4
Which next hop is chosen?
options: R1
R3
R2
R4
options_html: AR1
BR3
CR2
DR4
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Classless forwarding does not look for 'the' matching network; it looks for the match with the longest prefix, because that is the most specific statement about where the address lives.

Step by step.

  1. Against 10.1.0.0/16: the first 16 bits 10.1 match. Match, length 16.
  2. Against 10.1.32.0/20: the first 20 bits are 10.1.32.0/20 = 10.1.0010 0000, and 10.1.34.19 has third octet 34 = 0010 0010, whose first four bits 0010 match. Match, length 20.
  3. Against 10.1.34.0/24: the first 24 bits match exactly, since the third octet is 34 in both. Match, length 24.
  4. Against 0.0.0.0/0: default route, matches everything at length 0.
  5. Longest match is the /24, so the packet goes to R3.

Answer: Option (B) — R3.

Common misconception. Choosing R1 because the /16 'contains' the address ignores specificity. Choosing R4 because several routes match treats the table as ambiguous when it is not.

Takeaway. Longest prefix wins, always. The default route is simply the shortest possible match, /0.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: What is the directed broadcast address of the subnet 192.168.1.64/26?
questions.question_html:
Question 14MCQeasysubnet-masking-supernettingstandard textbookMarks: 1

What is the directed broadcast address of the subnet 192.168.1.64/26?
options_html: A192.168.1.63
B192.168.1.64
C192.168.1.127
D192.168.1.128
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The broadcast address of a subnet is its network address plus the block size minus one: the address whose host bits are all 1.

Step by step.

  1. Block size = 2^(32−26) = 64.
  2. The subnet starts at 192.168.1.64 and covers 64 addresses.
  3. Its last address is 64 + 64 − 1 = 127.
  4. So the broadcast is 192.168.1.127 and the usable hosts are .65 to .126.

Answer: Option (C) — 192.168.1.127.

Common misconception. 192.168.1.63 is the broadcast of the previous subnet, and 192.168.1.128 is the network address of the next one; both are boundary addresses of neighbours.

Takeaway. Broadcast = network address + block size − 1. The next subnet's network address is always broadcast + 1.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which dotted-decimal subnet mask corresponds to the prefix /28?
questions.question_html:
Question 15MCQeasysubnet-masking-supernettingstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which dotted-decimal subnet mask corresponds to the prefix /28?
options_html: A255.255.255.224
B255.255.255.192
C255.255.255.240
D255.255.255.248
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A /28 keeps 28 network bits and 4 host bits. The fourth octet therefore contributes 4 network bits, whose value is 240.

Step by step.

  1. First three octets are fully network: 255.255.255.
  2. Fourth octet has 4 leading 1s and 4 trailing 0s: 11110000₂ = 240.
  3. So the mask is 255.255.255.240, leaving 2⁴ = 16 addresses, of which 14 are usable.

Answer: Option (C) — 255.255.255.240.

Common misconception. 255.255.255.224 is /27 and 255.255.255.248 is /29. Mixing them up shifts the subnet size by a factor of two in either direction.

Takeaway. Fourth-octet masks: /25 = 128, /26 = 192, /27 = 224, /28 = 240, /29 = 248, /30 = 252.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A /16 network is divided into equal subnets, each with the mask 255.255.255.192. How many subnets are created?
questions.question_html:
Question 16NATeasysubnet-masking-supernettingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A /16 network is divided into equal subnets, each with the mask 255.255.255.192. How many subnets are created?

Answer format: an integer number of subnets.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Subnetting is borrowing bits from the host portion. The number of subnets is 2 raised to the number of borrowed bits.

Step by step.

  1. Mask 255.255.255.192 is /26, since the fourth octet holds two leading 1s beyond the /24 boundary.
  2. Borrowed bits = 26 − 16 = 10.
  3. Number of subnets = 2¹⁰ = 1024.
  4. Each subnet holds 2^(32−26) = 64 addresses, and 1024 × 64 = 65536 = 2¹⁶, the size of the original /16.

Answer: 1024 subnets.

Common misconception. Treating 255.255.255.192 as /27 gives 2048, and forgetting the /16 starting point gives 4. The check against the size of the original block catches both.

Takeaway. Borrowed bits b give 2^b subnets of 2^(remaining) addresses each, and the products must reconstruct the original block.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which single CIDR block summarizes exactly the eight networks 192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.7.0/24, with no extra address space?
questions.question_html:
Question 17MCQmediumsubnet-masking-supernettingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Which single CIDR block summarizes exactly the eight networks 192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.7.0/24, with no extra address space?
options_html: A192.168.0.0/21
B192.168.0.0/22
C192.168.0.0/20
D192.168.0.0/23
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Supernetting reverses subnetting: combine neighbouring blocks by removing network bits, and the block must begin on a boundary that is a multiple of its own size.

Step by step.

  1. Eight /24 blocks means 2³ = 8, so three bits must be released from the prefix.
  2. 24 − 3 = 21, so the candidate is a /21.
  3. A /21 covers 2^(32−21) = 2048 addresses = 8 × 256, matching the eight /24s exactly.
  4. The start address must be a multiple of the block size in the third octet: 0 is a multiple of 8, so 192.168.0.0/21 is aligned.
  5. A /22 covers only 4 of the eight blocks and a /23 only 2; a /20 covers 16, which adds eight networks that were not asked for.

Answer: Option (A) — 192.168.0.0/21.

Common misconception. A /20 is the usual wrong answer: it does cover all eight networks, but it also covers eight more, so it is not an exact summary. Alignment is the other trap: 192.168.4.0/21 would be invalid because 4 is not a multiple of 8.

Takeaway. To aggregate n blocks, remove log₂n bits, then confirm the first block is aligned to the new block size.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The network 172.16.0.0/16 is divided into equal /20 subnets. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 18MSQmediumsubnet-masking-supernettingstandard textbookMarks: 2

The network 172.16.0.0/16 is divided into equal /20 subnets. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Exactly 16 subnets are created.
Each subnet has 4094 usable host addresses.
172.16.40.0/20 is a valid subnet boundary of this network.
172.16.32.0/20 is a valid subnet of this network.
options_html: AExactly 16 subnets are created.
BEach subnet has 4094 usable host addresses.
C172.16.40.0/20 is a valid subnet boundary of this network.
D172.16.32.0/20 is a valid subnet of this network.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A /16 split into /20 subnets borrows four bits from the host portion. The subnet boundaries are then multiples of 2⁴ = 16 in the third octet.

Step by step.

  1. Borrowed bits = 20 − 16 = 4, so the number of subnets is 2⁴ = 16. (A) true.
  2. Host bits left = 32 − 20 = 12, so each subnet holds 2¹² = 4096 addresses and 4096 − 2 = 4094 usable hosts. (B) true.
  3. Valid boundaries in the third octet are multiples of 16: 0, 16, 32, 48, 64, ... and so on. 40 is not a multiple of 16, so 172.16.40.0/20 straddles two subnets and is invalid. (C) false.
  4. 32 is a multiple of 16, so 172.16.32.0/20 is the third subnet. (D) true.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (C) is the designed trap: 40 looks like a round number, but a /20 boundary must be a multiple of 16 in the third octet. Writing the boundary list out is the only safe check.

Takeaway. Subnet boundaries of a /20 are multiples of 16 in the third octet, because 2⁴ = 16.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Host A is configured as 10.1.2.3/22 and host B as 10.1.6.5/22. Which statement is correct?
questions.question_html:
Question 19MCQhardsubnet-masking-supernettingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Host A is configured as 10.1.2.3/22 and host B as 10.1.6.5/22. Which statement is correct?
options: They are on the same subnet, 10.1.0.0/22.
They are on the same subnet, 10.1.4.0/22.
They are on different subnets: 10.1.0.0/22 and 10.1.8.0/22.
They are on different subnets: 10.1.0.0/22 and 10.1.4.0/22.
options_html: AThey are on the same subnet, 10.1.0.0/22.
BThey are on the same subnet, 10.1.4.0/22.
CThey are on different subnets: 10.1.0.0/22 and 10.1.8.0/22.
DThey are on different subnets: 10.1.0.0/22 and 10.1.4.0/22.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two hosts share a subnet only if their addresses agree on every network bit of the prefix. A /22 takes six bits of the third octet, so subnets are 4 apart in that octet.

Step by step.

  1. Block size = 2^(32−22) = 2¹⁰ = 1024 addresses = 4 whole /24 blocks.
  2. Host A: third octet 2. The multiple of 4 not exceeding 2 is 0, so A lies in 10.1.0.0/22, covering 10.1.0.0 to 10.1.3.255.
  3. Host B: third octet 6. The multiple of 4 not exceeding 6 is 4, so B lies in 10.1.4.0/22, covering 10.1.4.0 to 10.1.7.255.
  4. The two subnets differ, so A is in 10.1.0.0/22 and B is in 10.1.4.0/22.
  5. Check by masking: 10.1.2.3 ∧ 255.255.252.0 = 10.1.0.0, while 10.1.6.5 ∧ 255.255.252.0 = 10.1.4.0.

Answer: Option (D) — different subnets, 10.1.0.0/22 and 10.1.4.0/22.

Common misconception. Option (A) assumes a /16-style view where everything under 10.1 is one network. Option (C) miscounts the block size as 8, which would be a /21.

Takeaway. Mask both addresses with the subnet mask and compare the results; never compare the addresses by eye.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The block 203.0.113.0/24 is allocated with VLSM: four departments receive the prefixes /27, /28, /29 and /30 respectively, and no address inside an allocated prefix is left unused. How many addresses of the /24 remain unallocated?
questions.question_html:
Question 20NAThardsubnet-masking-supernettingoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

The block 203.0.113.0/24 is allocated with VLSM: four departments receive the prefixes /27, /28, /29 and /30 respectively, and no address inside an allocated prefix is left unused. How many addresses of the /24 remain unallocated?

Answer format: an integer number of addresses.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. VLSM allocates blocks of different sizes from one address pool. The pool has 256 addresses; each allocation consumes 2^(32−prefix) of them, whatever the prefix.

Step by step.

  1. A /24 contains 2⁸ = 256 addresses.
  2. /27 consumes 2^(32−27) = 2⁵ = 32 addresses.
  3. /28 consumes 2⁴ = 16 addresses.
  4. /29 consumes 2³ = 8 addresses.
  5. /30 consumes 2² = 4 addresses.
  6. Total allocated = 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 = 60.
  7. Unallocated = 256 − 60 = 196 addresses.

Answer: 196 addresses.

Common misconception. Counting only usable hosts (30 + 14 + 6 + 2 = 52) and subtracting from 254 mixes two different bases. The question is about address space, so work in total addresses throughout.

Takeaway. VLSM arithmetic is in total addresses, not usable hosts. Convert every prefix to 2^(32−p) first.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: What is the fixed length of the IPv6 base header?
questions.question_html:
Question 21MCQeasyipv6-basics-differencesstandard textbookMarks: 1

What is the fixed length of the IPv6 base header?
options: 20 bytes
40 bytes
48 bytes
60 bytes
options_html: A20 bytes
B40 bytes
C48 bytes
D60 bytes
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. IPv6 deliberately fixes the base header length so that routers can parse it at a constant offset, moving all optional information into extension headers.

Step by step.

  1. The base header has a fixed layout of eight fields: Version, Traffic Class, Flow Label, Payload Length, Next Header, Hop Limit, Source Address and Destination Address.
  2. Source and destination addresses take 2 × 16 = 32 bytes.
  3. The remaining fields take 8 bytes.
  4. Total = 40 bytes, and there is no IHL field because the length never varies.

Answer: Option (B) — 40 bytes.

Common misconception. 20 bytes is the IPv4 minimum header, and 60 bytes is the IPv4 maximum. IPv6 has neither a variable base header nor an options field inside it.

Takeaway. IPv4: 20 to 60 bytes, variable, IHL present. IPv6: exactly 40 bytes, no IHL.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which field is present in the IPv4 header but has been removed from the IPv6 base header?
questions.question_html:
Question 22MCQeasyipv6-basics-differencesstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which field is present in the IPv4 header but has been removed from the IPv6 base header?
options: Header checksum
Hop Limit
Flow Label
Version
options_html: AHeader checksum
BHop Limit
CFlow Label
DVersion
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. IPv6 removed the header checksum because every link layer and every transport protocol already checks integrity, and recomputing a checksum at each hop was the dominant per-packet cost in IPv4 routers.

Step by step.

  1. Version exists in both: 4 in IPv4, 6 in IPv6.
  2. The hop count exists in both, renamed from TTL to Hop Limit in IPv6.
  3. Flow Label is new in IPv6 and has no IPv4 counterpart.
  4. The header checksum exists only in IPv4; IPv6 relies on link-layer and transport-layer checksums.

Answer: Option (A) — header checksum.

Common misconception. TTL is often guessed because the name changed, but the field itself survives as Hop Limit. Flow Label is the reverse mistake: it is an IPv6 addition, not an IPv4 field.

Takeaway. IPv6 dropped exactly two things from the base header: the checksum and the options/IHL mechanism, the latter replaced by extension headers.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about IPv6 are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 23MSQmediumipv6-basics-differencesstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about IPv6 are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The IPv6 base header carries no header checksum; error detection is delegated to the link and transport layers.
IPv6 routers may fragment a datagram that exceeds the next link's MTU.
The IPv6 base header is 20 bytes long.
IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long.
options_html: AThe IPv6 base header carries no header checksum; error detection is delegated to the link and transport layers.
BIPv6 routers may fragment a datagram that exceeds the next link's MTU.
CThe IPv6 base header is 20 bytes long.
DIPv6 addresses are 128 bits long.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. IPv6 keeps the network layer thin: routers forward without checksumming, without fragmenting, and without parsing options that do not concern them.

Step by step.

  1. (A) true. The header checksum was removed. Integrity is provided by the link layer (for example Ethernet FCS) and by the transport layer (UDP and TCP checksums, which are mandatory in IPv6).
  2. (B) false. In IPv6 only the source may fragment, and it does so by inserting a Fragment extension header. A router that meets an oversized datagram drops it and returns an ICMPv6 Packet Too Big message, which is how path MTU discovery works.
  3. (C) false. The IPv6 base header is a fixed 40 bytes; 20 bytes is the IPv4 minimum.
  4. (D) true. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits.

Answer: Options (A) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (B) is the central IPv6 misconception: people carry over IPv4's router fragmentation. IPv6 moves that job to the source, and routers only report the problem.

Takeaway. IPv6: no router fragmentation, no header checksum, fixed 40-byte base header, 128-bit addresses.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about IPv6 address notation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 24MSQmediumipv6-basics-differencesoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about IPv6 address notation are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A single address may contain two separate :: compressions.
::1 is the loopback address.
In 2001:db8::1/64, the first 64 bits form the network prefix.
A single :: may replace one run of consecutive all-zero groups.
options_html: AA single address may contain two separate :: compressions.
B::1 is the loopback address.
CIn 2001:db8::1/64, the first 64 bits form the network prefix.
DA single :: may replace one run of consecutive all-zero groups.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. IPv6 notation allows leading zeros in a group to be dropped and one run of zero groups to be compressed to ::, but only one such run, so that the expansion is unique.

Step by step.

  1. (A) false. Only one :: is allowed per address. With two, the reader could not tell how many zero groups belong to each run, so the address would be ambiguous. For example ::1::2 cannot be expanded uniquely.
  2. (B) true. ::1 expands to 0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001, the loopback address, the IPv6 counterpart of 127.0.0.1.
  3. (C) true. The /64 suffix states that 64 bits are the prefix; the remaining 64 bits are the interface identifier, which is why a /64 is the standard LAN size.
  4. (D) true. That is precisely what :: means: one maximal run of zero groups, as in 2001:db8::1 for 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (A) is the classic notation trap. A second common error is thinking :: may compress a run of zeros in the middle of a group; it only replaces whole 16-bit groups.

Takeaway. One :: per address, whole groups only. That rule is what makes the compressed form uniquely expandable.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An ISP delegates the prefix 2001:db8:abcd::/48 to a customer, who subdivides it into /64 subnets. How many /64 subnets can the customer create?
questions.question_html:
Question 25MCQhardipv6-basics-differencesoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

An ISP delegates the prefix 2001:db8:abcd::/48 to a customer, who subdivides it into /64 subnets. How many /64 subnets can the customer create?
options_html: A256
B1024
C4096
D65536
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The number of equal subnets obtainable from a delegated prefix is 2 raised to the difference in prefix lengths, exactly as in IPv4 CIDR.

Step by step.

  1. Delegated prefix length = 48; subnet prefix length = 64.
  2. Bits available for subnetting = 64 − 48 = 16.
  3. Number of /64s = 2¹⁶ = 65536.
  4. Check: a /48 holds 2¹²⁸ addresses and a /64 holds 2⁶⁴; the quotient is 2¹⁶.

Answer: Option (D) — 65536.

Common misconception. Applying the IPv4 habit of counting octets gives 2⁴ = 256 or 2¹² = 4096, but IPv6 prefixes are counted in bits and the gap here is 16 bits, not 8 or 12.

Takeaway. Subnet count = 2^(new prefix − delegated prefix), in IPv6 exactly as in IPv4.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: As an IPv4 datagram is forwarded by a router, which header field must the router recompute?
questions.question_html:
Question 1MCQeasyipv4-header-format-fragmentationstandard textbookMarks: 1

As an IPv4 datagram is forwarded by a router, which header field must the router recompute?
options: Header checksum
Total Length
Identification
Fragment offset
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The IPv4 header checksum covers the header only, and the header is modified in transit because the TTL is decremented at every router.

Step by step.

  1. The router decrements the TTL (Time To Live) field by one on every hop.
  2. That single change invalidates the checksum, which is computed over the whole header.
  3. The router therefore recomputes the header checksum before forwarding the datagram.
  4. Total Length changes only if the datagram is fragmented, and Identification and fragment offset are set once at the source and copied unchanged into every fragment.

Answer: Option (A) — the header checksum.

Common misconception. Total Length is the usual wrong answer, because fragmentation does change it — but only when a router actually fragments, not on every hop. Identification and fragment offset are never recomputed by a router.

Takeaway. The IPv4 header checksum is a per-hop check that exists only because the TTL changes; IPv6 removed both the field and the recomputation.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: What is the purpose of the 16-bit Identification field in an IPv4 header?
questions.question_html:
Question 2MCQeasyipv4-header-format-fragmentationstandard textbookMarks: 1

What is the purpose of the 16-bit Identification field in an IPv4 header?
options: It carries a sequence number that the receiving transport layer uses to detect loss.
It tags every fragment of one original datagram so that the destination can group them for reassembly.
It numbers the fragments in transmission order so that they can be put back in sequence.
It identifies the sending host uniquely along the path.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Reassembly needs two separate pieces of information: which fragments belong to the same original datagram, and where each one sits inside it. The Identification field supplies the first; the fragment offset supplies the second.

Step by step.

  1. When a router fragments a datagram, every fragment copies the original Identification value.
  2. The destination collects fragments that share source, destination, protocol and Identification value.
  3. The fragment offset places each fragment's payload at the correct position, and the MF flag marks the last fragment.
  4. Ordering is therefore by fragment offset, not by arrival order, which is why option (B) is wrong.

Answer: Option (B) — membership, not position.

Common misconception. Option (C) is the trap: the field looks like a sequence number. It is not one, because all fragments carry the same Identification value; the position information lives in the fragment offset field.

Takeaway. Identification = membership; fragment offset = position; MF = end marker. All three are needed for reassembly.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An IPv4 datagram carries 12 bytes of options in its header. It must cross a link whose MTU is 1500 bytes. Every fragment except the last carries the largest payload that keeps the fragment offset legal. What is the payload size, in bytes, of each such fragment?
questions.question_html:
Question 3NATmediumipv4-header-format-fragmentationstandard textbookMarks: 2

An IPv4 datagram carries 12 bytes of options in its header. It must cross a link whose MTU is 1500 bytes. Every fragment except the last carries the largest payload that keeps the fragment offset legal. What is the payload size, in bytes, of each such fragment?

Answer format: an integer number of bytes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The MTU bounds the whole datagram, header included, so the payload room per fragment is MTU minus the full header. The payload must also be a multiple of 8 bytes, because the fragment offset counts 8-byte units.

Step by step.

  1. The header is 20 fixed bytes plus 12 bytes of options, so 32 bytes in total. Options are copied into every fragment.
  2. Payload room = 1500 − 32 = 1468 bytes.
  3. 1468 / 8 = 183.5, which is not a whole number of 8-byte units, so the largest legal payload is 183 × 8 = 1464 bytes.
  4. The 4 leftover bytes are simply not used by a non-final fragment.

Answer: 1464 bytes per fragment.

Common misconception. Two errors dominate: using 1480 bytes, which forgets that options are copied into every fragment, and using 1468 bytes, which forgets that the payload must be a multiple of 8.

Takeaway. Payload room = MTU − (20 + options), then round down to a multiple of 8.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A fragment arrives with fragment offset 185 and the MF flag set to 1. At which byte of the original datagram's payload does this fragment's own payload begin?
questions.question_html:
Question 4MCQmediumipv4-header-format-fragmentationoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A fragment arrives with fragment offset 185 and the MF flag set to 1. At which byte of the original datagram's payload does this fragment's own payload begin?
options: Byte 185
Byte 1479
Byte 1480
Byte 1488
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The fragment offset field counts the position of a fragment's payload in units of 8 bytes, measured from the first byte of the original payload.

Step by step.

  1. One offset unit = 8 bytes.
  2. 185 units × 8 bytes = 1480 bytes.
  3. Offsets are measured from the first byte of the original payload, which is byte 0.
  4. So this fragment begins at byte 1480, and MF = 1 tells the destination that more fragments follow.

Answer: Option (C) — byte 1480.

Common misconception. Reporting 185 reads the field as a byte count; reporting 1488 adds a spurious 8 bytes by treating the byte numbering as 1-based.

Takeaway. Byte position = fragment offset × 8. Convert once, at the start of the calculation.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation and reassembly are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 5MSQmediumipv4-header-format-fragmentationstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about IPv4 fragmentation and reassembly are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Reassembly is performed only at the final destination; routers forward fragments but never reassemble them.
Every fragment produced from one original datagram carries the same Identification value.
A fragment's Total Length field counts that fragment's own IPv4 header as well as its payload.
The fragment offset field is measured in bytes of the original payload.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Fragmentation is a source-and-router activity; reassembly is an end-host activity. Each fragment is itself a complete datagram, carrying its own header, so its Total Length includes that header.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — a router that reassembled would have to hold state and would defeat the design; reassembly happens at the destination.
  2. (B) True — Identification is copied into every fragment so that the destination can group them.
  3. (C) True — each fragment is a datagram in its own right, so Total Length counts header plus payload of that fragment.
  4. (D) False — the offset counts 8-byte units, not bytes, which is exactly why every non-final fragment's payload must be a multiple of 8.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Option (D) is the standard slip: the field is often called a 'byte offset'. It is an offset in 8-byte units, and reading it as bytes understates the position by a factor of eight.

Takeaway. Every fragment is a whole datagram; the three fields that hold the pieces together are Identification, MF and fragment offset.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An IPv4 datagram of total length 4500 bytes (20-byte header, no options) must cross a link whose MTU is 1000 bytes. Every fragment except the last is filled to the largest legal multiple of 8 bytes. How many fragments are produced, and what is the fragment offset of the last fragment?
questions.question_html:
Question 6MCQhardipv4-header-format-fragmentationoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

An IPv4 datagram of total length 4500 bytes (20-byte header, no options) must cross a link whose MTU is 1000 bytes. Every fragment except the last is filled to the largest legal multiple of 8 bytes. How many fragments are produced, and what is the fragment offset of the last fragment?
options: 5 fragments, last offset 3904
5 fragments, last offset 488
4 fragments, last offset 488
6 fragments, last offset 585
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two numbers have to be kept apart: the payload room per fragment, which is MTU minus header rounded down to a multiple of 8, and the fragment offset, which is that payload divided by 8.

Step by step.

  1. Payload to be carried = 4500 − 20 = 4480 bytes.
  2. Payload room per fragment = 1000 − 20 = 980, rounded down to 976 bytes (976 = 122 × 8).
  3. 4480 = 4 × 976 + 576, so four full fragments carry 3904 bytes and the last fragment carries the remaining 576 bytes: 5 fragments in total.
  4. Offsets are 0, 122, 244, 366 and 488, so the last fragment's offset is 488.

Answer: Option (B) — 5 fragments with the last fragment offset equal to 488.

Common misconception. Option (A) reports 3904, which is the byte position of the last fragment rather than the value of the offset field; the field counts 8-byte units, so 3904 / 8 = 488. Option (D) comes from treating 1000 bytes as the payload per fragment, which ignores the header.

Takeaway. Count full fragments with 976-byte payloads, then convert the byte position to 8-byte units for the offset field.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A datagram with a 20-byte header carries 3000 bytes of payload and must cross a link with MTU 800 bytes. Every fragment except the last is filled to the largest legal multiple of 8 bytes. Give the fragment offset value, in 8-byte units, of the last fragment.
questions.question_html:
Question 7NAThardipv4-header-format-fragmentationoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A datagram with a 20-byte header carries 3000 bytes of payload and must cross a link with MTU 800 bytes. Every fragment except the last is filled to the largest legal multiple of 8 bytes. Give the fragment offset value, in 8-byte units, of the last fragment.

Answer format: an integer (the fragment offset value).
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The fragment offset of the last fragment equals the number of full fragments multiplied by the payload carried by each, all divided by 8.

Step by step.

  1. Payload room per fragment = 800 − 20 = 780 bytes, rounded down to 776 bytes (776 = 97 × 8).
  2. 3000 = 3 × 776 + 672, since 3 × 776 = 2328 and 3000 − 2328 = 672.
  3. So there are four fragments, with offsets 0, 97, 194 and 291.
  4. The last fragment starts 2328 bytes into the original payload, and 2328 / 8 = 291.

Answer: 291.

Common misconception. Reporting 672 gives the size of the last fragment, not its offset; reporting 390 understates the count by using 780 bytes per fragment, which is not a multiple of 8 and therefore illegal.

Takeaway. Last offset = (number of full fragments × payload per fragment) / 8.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: In classful IPv4 addressing, to which class does the address 240.1.2.3 belong?
questions.question_html:
Question 8MCQeasyclassful-vs-classless-cidrstandard textbookMarks: 1

In classful IPv4 addressing, to which class does the address 240.1.2.3 belong?
options: Class A
Class C
Class D
Class E
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The class of a classful address is fixed by its first octet: A 0–127, B 128–191, C 192–223, D 224–239 and E 240–255.

Step by step.

  1. The first octet is 240.
  2. 240 lies in the range 240–255, which is class E.
  3. Class D (224–239) is reserved for multicast, and class E is reserved for experimental use, so neither is assigned to ordinary hosts.
  4. The remaining three octets play no part in deciding the class.

Answer: Option (D) — Class E.

Common misconception. Class D is the common error, because 224–239 feels 'high'. The boundary is exact: 239 is the last class D address and 240 is the first class E address.

Takeaway. The first octet alone decides the class; memorise the five boundaries, not the class names.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: In classful addressing, how many bits of a Class B address form the host portion?
questions.question_html:
Question 9MCQeasyclassful-vs-classless-cidrstandard textbookMarks: 1

In classful addressing, how many bits of a Class B address form the host portion?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A classful address is split into a network portion fixed by the class and a host portion made up of everything that is left of the 32 bits.

Step by step.

  1. A Class B address starts with the bit pattern 10 and uses the first two octets for the network.
  2. That is 16 network bits, so the default mask is 255.255.0.0, or /16.
  3. The host portion is therefore 32 − 16 = 16 bits.
  4. 16 host bits give 2⁶⁶ − 2 = 65534 usable host addresses per Class B network.

Answer: Option (C) — 16 bits.

Common misconception. 14 is the trap: the first two bits of a Class B address are fixed at 10, and candidates sometimes subtract them from the 16 network bits instead of leaving the host bits alone.

Takeaway. Host bits by class: A 24, B 16, C 8. Usable hosts are 2 to that power, minus two.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The block 192.168.0.0/22 is assigned to a single organisation. How many usable host addresses does the block provide?
questions.question_html:
Question 10NATeasyclassful-vs-classless-cidrstandard textbookMarks: 2

The block 192.168.0.0/22 is assigned to a single organisation. How many usable host addresses does the block provide?

Answer format: an integer number of addresses.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A /p block contains 2^(32−p) addresses, of which the first is the network address and the last is the directed broadcast address, so two are not usable by hosts.

Step by step.

  1. Host bits = 32 − 22 = 10.
  2. Total addresses = 2¹⁰ = 1024.
  3. Subtract the network address (192.168.0.0) and the directed broadcast address (192.168.3.255).
  4. Usable addresses = 1024 − 2 = 1022.

Answer: 1022.

Common misconception. Reporting 1024 forgets the two reserved addresses; reporting 1023 forgets only one of them. Both appear as distractors in real papers.

Takeaway. Usable hosts in a /p block = 2^(32−p) − 2 for every prefix shorter than /31.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An organisation owns 172.16.0.0/16 and must carve it into equal subnets, all with the same mask, each supporting at least 4000 usable host addresses. What is the longest prefix that still satisfies the requirement?
questions.question_html:
Question 11MCQmediumclassful-vs-classless-cidroriginal synthesisMarks: 1

An organisation owns 172.16.0.0/16 and must carve it into equal subnets, all with the same mask, each supporting at least 4000 usable host addresses. What is the longest prefix that still satisfies the requirement?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The requirement is on usable hosts, so it is the host bits that must be sized first: 2^h − 2 must be at least the number of hosts required.

Step by step.

  1. We need 2^h − 2 ≥ 4000, that is 2^h ≥ 4002.
  2. 2¹¹ = 524288, 2¹₀ = 262144, 2¹₁ = 2046 usable hosts (too few), 2¹² = 4094 usable hosts (enough).
  3. So h = 12 host bits, and the prefix is 32 − 12 = /20.
  4. A /19 would also satisfy the requirement but is shorter, and the question asks for the longest prefix that still works.

Answer: Option (D) — /20.

Common misconception. Options (A), (B) and (C) all provide more than 4000 usable hosts, so all three would technically work; the question asks for the longest prefix, which is the smallest block that still fits. Candidates who round 4000 up to 4096 and stop at /19 pick (C) and lose the point.

Takeaway. Size the host bits from usable hosts (2^h − 2), then set prefix = 32 − h.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about classless addressing and CIDR are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 12MSQmediumclassful-vs-classless-cidrstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about classless addressing and CIDR are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A CIDR block is written as address/prefix with any prefix length from /0 to /32, so the old class boundaries no longer constrain the mask.
A /p block contains 2^(32−p) addresses.
Classless addressing forbids subnetting a block that has already been subnetted.
Several contiguous blocks can be advertised as one aggregate route, which shrinks routing tables.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. CIDR replaced the fixed class boundaries with an explicit prefix length, which is what makes both arbitrary subdivision and aggregation possible.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — the prefix length is carried with the address, so any value from /0 to /32 is legal.
  2. (B) True — the prefix fixes the network bits and the rest are host bits, giving 2^(32−p) addresses.
  3. (C) False — a classless block can be subnetted as many times as the owner likes, and that is exactly how VLSM works.
  4. (D) True — aggregation of contiguous blocks into a shorter prefix is the main reason CIDR was introduced.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (C) confuses classless addressing with classful rules: classful addressing did restrict subnetting of an already-subnetted network to a single mask, and CIDR removed that restriction.

Takeaway. CIDR = explicit prefix length + aggregation. Both halves of that sentence are examinable.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A host is configured as 10.10.10.10/12. What is the last usable host address of the subnet it belongs to?
questions.question_html:
Question 13MCQhardclassful-vs-classless-cidroriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A host is configured as 10.10.10.10/12. What is the last usable host address of the subnet it belongs to?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. For a prefix shorter than /24 the block boundary falls inside the second octet, so the second octet must be masked first; the broadcast address is then the last address of the block.

Step by step.

  1. /12 means a mask of 255.240.0.0, so the block size in the second octet is 16.
  2. 10 AND 240 = 0, so the network address is 10.0.0.0/12.
  3. The block therefore spans 10.0.0.0 to 10.15.255.255; the last address is the directed broadcast address.
  4. The last usable host address is one below it: 10.15.255.254.

Answer: Option (B) — 10.15.255.254.

Common misconception. Option (A) takes the broadcast address itself, which is never usable; option (C) treats the prefix as /8 and takes the second octet as host bits; option (D) keeps the 10 of the original address in the second octet, which the /12 mask clears.

Takeaway. Mask the octet that contains the boundary first; the broadcast address is the last address of that block, and the last usable host is one below it.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which prefix length corresponds to the subnet mask 255.255.255.224?
questions.question_html:
Question 14MCQeasysubnet-masking-supernettingstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which prefix length corresponds to the subnet mask 255.255.255.224?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A prefix length is the count of leading 1 bits in the mask, so each octet value must be read as a run of 1s followed by 0s.

Step by step.

  1. The first three octets are all 255, which is 24 ones.
  2. 224 in binary is 1110 0000, which is three more ones.
  3. 24 + 3 = /27.
  4. Equivalently, the block size is 256 − 224 = 32, and 32 = 2⁵ corresponds to 5 host bits, so the prefix is 32 − 5 = 27.

Answer: Option (C) — /27.

Common misconception. /26 (mask 192) and /28 (mask 240) are the neighbouring values, and candidates who count the 1s in 224 as four rather than three land on /28.

Takeaway. Mask value to prefix: count the 1 bits in the non-255 octet, or use block size = 256 − mask.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: An interface is configured as 192.168.5.205/29. What is the subnet (network) address of its subnet?
questions.question_html:
Question 15MCQeasysubnet-masking-supernettingstandard textbookMarks: 1

An interface is configured as 192.168.5.205/29. What is the subnet (network) address of its subnet?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A subnet address is obtained by clearing the host bits, which for a prefix inside the last octet means rounding the last octet down to a multiple of the block size.

Step by step.

  1. /29 leaves 3 host bits, so the block size is 2³ = 8.
  2. The subnet boundaries in the last octet are multiples of 8: 192, 200, 208 and so on.
  3. 205 lies between 200 and 207, so the subnet address is 192.168.5.200.
  4. The broadcast address of that subnet is 192.168.5.207, and the usable hosts are 201 to 206.

Answer: Option (A) — 192.168.5.200.

Common misconception. Option (B) uses a block size of 4, which is a /30; option (C) rounds up to the next multiple of 8 instead of down. Both come from misreading the prefix rather than from an arithmetic slip.

Takeaway. Block size = 2^(32−prefix); the subnet address is the largest multiple of the block size that does not exceed the host address.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: How many /26 subnets can be carved out of the block 10.0.0.0/22?
questions.question_html:
Question 16NATmediumsubnet-masking-supernettingstandard textbookMarks: 2

How many /26 subnets can be carved out of the block 10.0.0.0/22?

Answer format: an integer number of subnets.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Subdividing a /p block into /q subnets uses q − p extra network bits, which yields 2^(q−p) subnets of equal size.

Step by step.

  1. The given block is /22 and the target subnet is /26.
  2. Extra network bits borrowed = 26 − 22 = 4.
  3. Number of subnets = 2⁴ = 16.
  4. Each subnet then holds 2⁶ = 64 addresses, and 16 × 64 = 1024, which is exactly the size of a /22 block.

Answer: 16 subnets.

Common misconception. Reporting 4 counts the borrowed bits rather than the subnets; reporting 64 confuses the number of subnets with the number of addresses inside one subnet.

Takeaway. Subnets = 2^(new prefix − old prefix). Check the total addresses match as a sanity test.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which pair of /25 blocks aggregates into exactly one /24 with no extra address space?
questions.question_html:
Question 17MCQmediumsubnet-masking-supernettingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Which pair of /25 blocks aggregates into exactly one /24 with no extra address space?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two blocks aggregate exactly when they are the two halves of one larger block: they must share every prefix bit above the aggregate length and differ only in the bit that the aggregate fixes.

Step by step.

  1. A /24 splits into exactly two /25 halves: the one with bit 25 equal to 0 and the one with bit 25 equal to 1.
  2. For 200.1.2.0/24 those halves are 200.1.2.0/25 (addresses .0 to .127) and 200.1.2.128/25 (addresses .128 to .255).
  3. Their union is the whole /24, so they aggregate with no waste.
  4. Option (B) and option (C) each span two different /24 blocks and cannot be summarised by one /24; option (D) pairs a valid /25 with 200.1.2.192/25, which is not even a legal /25 boundary because 192 is a /26 boundary.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Any two /25s feel summarisable, but the blocks must be siblings. A pair straddling two /24s would leave a hole, so the aggregate would have to be a /23 covering address space the organisation does not own.

Takeaway. Aggregate only siblings: identical prefix bits above the aggregate length, differing only in the bits the aggregate fixes.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following statements about VLSM and supernetting are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 18MSQmediumsubnet-masking-supernettingstandard textbookMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about VLSM and supernetting are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: VLSM allows the subnets carved from one address block to use different prefix lengths.
In a VLSM design, allocating the largest subnets first keeps the remaining space contiguous and usable.
Every subnet in a VLSM design must use the same mask.
Route summarisation works best when the subnets of a block are contiguous and aligned to their own block sizes.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. VLSM is the freedom to subnet a block repeatedly with different prefix lengths, and its practical success depends on allocating in descending size order so that no large block is split by a small one.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — that freedom is the definition of VLSM.
  2. (B) True — a small subnet placed inside a large block's address range destroys that block's alignment, so the large ones must be placed first.
  3. (C) False — a single mask is fixed-length subnetting, which is precisely what VLSM replaces.
  4. (D) True — contiguous, aligned blocks share prefix bits above the aggregate length, which is the condition for exact summarisation.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Option (C) restates fixed-length subnetting and is the usual error, because many candidates learn subnetting as 'all subnets get the same mask' before meeting VLSM.

Takeaway. VLSM = different masks in one block; allocate largest first; aggregate only contiguous, aligned blocks.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The block 172.16.0.0/16 must be divided into equal subnets, all with the same mask, each providing at least 500 usable host addresses. What is the largest number of such subnets?
questions.question_html:
Question 19MCQhardsubnet-masking-supernettingoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

The block 172.16.0.0/16 must be divided into equal subnets, all with the same mask, each providing at least 500 usable host addresses. What is the largest number of such subnets?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The host requirement fixes the subnet size, and the subnet size fixes how many subnets fit in the parent block; maximising the count means choosing the smallest subnet that still meets the host requirement.

Step by step.

  1. We need 2^h − 2 ≥ 500, that is 2^h ≥ 502.
  2. 2⁹ = 512, giving 510 usable hosts, so h = 9 and the subnet prefix is 32 − 9 = /23.
  3. The number of /23 subnets in a /16 block is 2^(23−16) = 2⁷ = 128.
  4. A /24 subnet would give only 254 usable hosts, too few; a /22 would give more than needed but only 64 subnets.

Answer: Option (A) — 128 subnets.

Common misconception. Option (B) is the /24 count, and a /24 gives only 254 usable hosts, below the 500 required, so it cannot be used at all. Option (D) comes from sizing to a /22 and then counting its subnets.

Takeaway. Smallest legal subnet gives the largest count: solve 2^h − 2 ≥ hosts, then count subnets as 2^(q − p).

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: The IPv6 Next Header field carries out the job of which IPv4 header field?
questions.question_html:
Question 20MCQeasyipv6-basics-differencesstandard textbookMarks: 1

The IPv6 Next Header field carries out the job of which IPv4 header field?
options: Total Length
Header checksum
Identification
Protocol
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. IPv6 keeps one field whose job is to name what follows the current header. In the base header that is the upper-layer protocol; in an extension header it is the next extension header.

Step by step.

  1. In IPv4, the Protocol field holds a number such as 6 for TCP or 17 for UDP.
  2. In IPv6 the same number appears in the Next Header field of the base header.
  3. Unlike IPv4, the chain can continue: if the Next Header value names an extension header, that header carries its own Next Header field pointing further on.
  4. So Next Header generalises the Protocol field rather than replacing its meaning.

Answer: Option (D) — Protocol.

Common misconception. Option (B) is a frequent answer because IPv6's header differences are usually taught as a list of removals; the checksum was removed, not replaced by Next Header.

Takeaway. Next Header = IPv4 Protocol, extended into a chain through optional extension headers.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: Which of the following is the correctly compressed form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
questions.question_html:
Question 21MCQeasyipv6-basics-differencesstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which of the following is the correctly compressed form of 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001?
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two rules govern IPv6 text compression: leading zeros inside a group are dropped, and one run of all-zero groups may be replaced by a double colon, at most once.

Step by step.

  1. Dropping leading zeros in each group gives 2001:db8:0:0:0:0:0:1.
  2. The longest run of all-zero groups is five groups long (the third through seventh).
  3. Replacing that run with :: gives 2001:db8::1.
  4. The double colon may appear only once, so option (A) is illegal; option (C) moves 1 into the wrong group, which changes the address; option (D) keeps leading zeros and compresses nothing.

Answer: Option (C) — 2001:db8::1.

Common misconception. Option (B) is the trap for candidates who count groups from the wrong end: 2001:db8:1:: expands to 2001:0db8:0001:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000, a completely different address.

Takeaway. Drop leading zeros; compress exactly one run of zero groups; never write :: twice.

questions.subject: computer-networks
questions.question: A fully expanded IPv6 address is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits. How many hexadecimal digits does the address contain in total?
questions.question_html:
Question 22NATeasyipv6-basics-differencesstandard textbookMarks: 2

A fully expanded IPv6 address is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits. How many hexadecimal digits does the address contain in total?

Answer format: an integer number of hexadecimal digits.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The length of the address in digits follows directly from its structure: eight groups, four digits each, and each hexadecimal digit carries four bits.

Step by step.
